rationale:
Today's slate is built around the playbook's one long-form format that is working (a new drug name with fresh, peer-reviewed data and few competing explainers), plus Shorts that each add a new fact.

**Why petrelintide is the long-form (L1).** The radar's top item, retatrutide for sleep apnea, can't be a long-form today, for three reasons:
- **Repeat ban.** We made a Short on this topic on 10-24, and long-forms that repeat a Short from the last 14 days are banned.
- **Conflicting dates.** Our 10-24 brief says NEJM published on Oct 20; the radar says Oct 24.
- **Breaking news.** It's a news story, and fast-moving stories keep failing the long-form fact-check.

The other long-form options were weaker:
- **Stopping GLP-1s:** too close to our 09-29 long-form and 10-19 carousel (within 30 days).
- **Lane A:** already used 4 times this week against a target of 3.
- **Lane B (gray-market):** paused after 5 views.

So L1 is the playbook's 'What Is [new drug]?' pipeline test on petrelintide. It has a Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Phase 2 paper, picked up by Medical News Today on Oct 24, and almost no YouTube explainers. That's the same pattern that made EloraTZP work (499 views). Most of the video is settled science: amylin physiology, the history of pramlintide, and how this drug differs from GLP-1s. Only one segment covers trial results, and those come from the paper. It's logged as a pipeline-explainer test (not Lane C, because the paper is older than 48 hours) and scored against the Lane C median of 47.

**Shorts.**
- **S1 (13:00 lead):** new retatrutide kidney data from TRANSCEND-CKD. Retatrutide is our highest-peaking name, and no other channel has a consumer explainer yet.
- **S2 (08:00):** the 'honest uncertainty' bones Short. It's a test the playbook asked for, it's tirzepatide-first, and it suits women 50+.
- **S3 (20:00 funnel):** spin-off of L1, naming its exact title once L1 is live.

**Gray-market and recall options skipped:**
- The Penn Reddit study was already our 10-16 Short.
- The bodega lab tests repeat our 10-22 CBS Short.
- The Apothecary Pharma recall was our 10-21 Short.

**Also skipped:**
- **Muscle:** covered 5 times since 10-05.
- **Orforglipron:** it underperforms, and we covered it on 10-16.

**C1** reuses only the verified 10-20 'Tirzepatide Not Working Yet?' Short text, as the playbook requires. Drop it if that Short isn't confirmed as published.

**Balance:**
- **Pillars:** research ×2 (L1, S3), beyond-weight ×1, myths ×1, life-on-glp1 ×1.
- **Body systems:** kidney, bone, and appetite/weight.
- **Mix:** 4 emerging pieces, 1 evergreen, and 1 myth or uncertainty correction.

**Scheduling flag:** our 10-24 plan put the tirzepatide nausea spin-off at 20:00 tonight. If it's still queued, run S3 tomorrow at 20:00 instead so the two don't collide. S3 names L1 either way.

pieces.topic: Petrelintide (Roche/Zealand), a weekly amylin-analogue shot: how amylin differs from GLP-1, and what the Phase 2 ZUPREME-1 trial showed (Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, Oct 2026)
pieces.angle: Title: 'What Is Petrelintide? The Amylin Weight-Loss Shot Explained' (OK). Credit the source as 'The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, published online around 30 Sep 2026 (Zealand release, 30 Sep 2026)'; confirm the exact online date on the paper. Headline number: '9.0 mg petrelintide, the trial's highest arm: about 10.7% average weight loss at 42 weeks versus 1.7% on placebo (efficacy estimand; 10.2% treatment-policy)', with per-arm n from the paper. Nausea line: 'Across all petrelintide doses combined, 20% had nausea (79 of 404) versus 6% on placebo.' Say vomiting and GI discontinuations are zero only 'at the highest dose, per Zealand'. Status line: 'Investigational. Not approved by the FDA, MHRA, Health Canada or TGA as of 25 Oct 2026. Zealand and Roche say a Phase 3 programme (ZUPREME) has started.' Give dates only from ClinicalTrials.gov or company releases (e.g. ZUPREME-2, NCT06926842). Keep 'smaller than tirzepatide's in separate trials, not head-to-head'. Keep pramlintide label wording without doses. Keep the prescriber line, 'not personal advice' and 'don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own'.
pieces.working_title: What Is Petrelintide? The Amylin Weight-Loss Shot Explained
pieces.why: Tests the playbook's under-covered pipeline-drug hypothesis behind EloraTZP (499). The name is new, competition is low, mainstream press picked it up on Oct 24, and a peer-reviewed paper plus settled amylin physiology give the depth a long-form needs to pass the fact-check. | fact-check: The topic is valid and fits the pipeline-explainer test. Checked against the Zealand release on BioSpace (Sep 30, 2026), the Lancet D&E abstract record PIIS2213-8587(26)00213-5 and press coverage. Three things in the plan need fixing. (1) Date: the paper was published around Sep 30, 2026, alongside EASD 2026, not in October. (2) Status: Zealand and Roche say a global Phase 3 ZUPREME programme 'has been initiated', so 'Phase 2' on its own is out of date. (3) Nausea: 19.6% (79 of 404) is pooled across all five petrelintide doses (1.0, 2.5, 5.0, 7.0 and 9.0 mg). Placebo is 5 people (6%, consistent with 6.2%, but confirm the placebo n from the paper). The 10.7% is the 9.0 mg arm against 1.7% on placebo at week 42 under the efficacy estimand. Under the treatment-policy estimand it's 10.2%; state both. The release reports 485 adults analysed (493 enrolled), mean BMI 36.7, mean age 47, 53% female. Per-arm n must come from the paper. The Lancet page returned 403 to the fetcher, so the scriptwriter must confirm per-arm n and the population wording from the paper itself. The 'no vomiting and no GI discontinuations' claim applies only 'at the maximally effective dose' (Zealand wording); keep that scope. The watch-next video is already published, so naming it is fine, but don't echo its 'beat' frame in L1's own narration. Petrelintide is not a GLP-1 drug: the series name is fine, but say so out loud. Don't name dose strengths as advice; trial arm labels only.

pieces.topic: Retatrutide and the kidneys: TRANSCEND-CKD, a 24-week trial in adults with obesity and chronic kidney disease (HCPLive, Oct 22, 2026)
pieces.angle: Hook: 'Can retatrutide protect the kidneys?' Answer: 'In a 24-week trial presented at ASN Kidney Week (Oct 2026, reported by HCPLive on 22 Oct 2026), people with a baseline urine albumin of 30 or more saw it fall about 54% on retatrutide versus 9% on placebo. That's a placebo-adjusted difference of 49.2%.' Define UACR as 'urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, an early sign of kidney strain'. Population: 'adults with BMI 27 or higher and chronic kidney disease, with or without type 2 diabetes; 75 on retatrutide, 71 on placebo'. Then: 'No significant difference in measured kidney filtration. This is an early marker, not proof it prevents kidney failure. A large Phase 3 trial, TRIUMPH-Outcomes, is testing heart and kidney outcomes, with results expected around 2029 per ClinicalTrials.gov.' Status: 'Investigational, not approved anywhere as of 25 Oct 2026.' GI line: 'In earlier retatrutide trials, nausea and diarrhoea were common.' Never mention online products; for approved options or a trial, ask a prescriber; then 'not personal advice', the prescriber line, and 'follow for more'. On screen: 'early marker · 24 weeks · baseline UACR ≥30 subgroup · not kidney-failure outcomes · investigational'. 170 words or fewer.
pieces.working_title: Can Retatrutide Protect the Kidneys? What 24 Weeks Showed #shorts
pieces.why: Fresh Phase 2 data on our highest-peaking Shorts name (253, 196, 120) that only clinician press has covered so far. It adds a fact we haven't published: retatrutide and kidney markers. | fact-check: Verified via HCPLive (TRANSCEND-CKD, presented at ASN Kidney Week, Oct 21–25, 2026, Denver) and NCT05936151. What's wrong in the plan: (a) The population is adults with BMI 27 or higher and established CKD, with or without type 2 diabetes, and cystatin C eGFR 25–75. That is not just 'obesity'. (b) Group sizes are 75 on retatrutide (escalated to 12 mg) and 71 on placebo. (c) In HCPLive, the −49.2% is the placebo-adjusted difference among people with baseline UACR ≥30 mg/g (−53.7% versus −8.8%). It is not a separate overall figure, so present one number, not two. (d) For GFR, say 'no significant difference between groups in measured GFR', not 'didn't change'. (e) TRIUMPH-Outcomes isn't in HCPLive. Credit it to ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06383390 instead: Phase 3, about 10,000 adults with BMI 27 or higher and heart/blood-vessel disease and/or CKD, cardiovascular and kidney outcomes, estimated primary completion Feb 2029. (f) HCPLive doesn't report nausea or diarrhoea for this trial, so the GI line must be credited to retatrutide's earlier trials or dropped. (g) This is a conference presentation, not a peer-reviewed paper; say 'presented at'.

pieces.topic: Do tirzepatide and semaglutide affect bones? New systematic review of GLP-1 RA skeletal effects in adults with overweight or obesity (Arch Osteoporos, Oct 23, 2026)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Do Semaglutide and Other GLP-1 Shots Affect Your Bones?' (no tirzepatide in the title). Open with the planned calm question. Body: 'A systematic review published on 23 Oct 2026 in Archives of Osteoporosis pooled 8 small randomized trials in adults with overweight or obesity (confirm the n from the abstract). Mostly exenatide and liraglutide, with only one semaglutide trial. Tirzepatide wasn't included. The certainty of evidence was very low, and the authors say it's too thin to tell whether these drugs help, spare or harm bone. Fracture trials are needed.' Then: 'Losing weight by any method can come with some bone loss.' Habits (general advice, not proven on the drug): muscle-strengthening at least 2 days a week, started gently, and a protein food at each meal unless your clinician has told you to limit protein. If you have osteoporosis or fracture risk, ask your clinician about bone health. One GI line (nausea is common). 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.' 'Not personal advice' plus the prescriber line. No scare visuals.
pieces.working_title: Do Tirzepatide or Semaglutide Affect Your Bones? #shorts
pieces.why: Runs the body-worry test the playbook asked for (macular degeneration: 104 on YouTube, 160 on Instagram). The review is brand new with low competition, and the topic suits women 50+ worried about menopause and bones. | fact-check: The review exists: Lai C-H et al., 'Skeletal effects of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in adults with overweight or obesity: a systematic review', Archives of Osteoporosis 2026; 21:148, published 23 Oct 2026, DOI 10.1007/s11657-026-01785-8. Per secondary coverage it included 8 RCTs (about 493 participants) covering exenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide and semaglutide (1 trial). GRADE certainty was very low for every agent, and the conclusion was that the evidence is too sparse and too heterogeneous to establish skeletal effects. **Tirzepatide was not included.** That makes the working title, which names tirzepatide, misleading. The per-agent trial counts add up to 9 against 8 trials and the participant total needs checking, so confirm both against the Springer abstract before using them. Don't say 'no effect'; the review says the evidence can't tell. The habit advice and the clinician caveat are fine.
